title: Can You Be Too Focused on Ministry and Forget God?
paragraphs: Can You Be Too Focused on Ministry and Forget God?
There is a tragedy that rarely gets preached because it hides behind applause.
It does not look like rebellion.
It does not look like backsliding.
It does not look like unbelief.
In fact, it often looks like faithfulness.
It looks like serving.
Leading.
Teaching.
Preaching.
Volunteering.
Building.
Giving.
Organizing.
Creating.
Helping everyone else encounter God while quietly drifting away from Him yourself.
The frightening reality is that a person can become so consumed with the work of God that they slowly neglect the presence of God.
And the most dangerous part?
Most people will congratulate them while it happens.
The church may celebrate them.
Friends may admire them.
Followers may applaud them.
Yet deep inside, something sacred is fading.
The intimacy is gone.
The wonder is gone.
The tears during prayer are gone.
The hunger for Scripture is gone.
The secret place has become a storage room for old memories.
Many believers fear failure.
Far fewer fear success.
Yet success in ministry without intimacy with God has destroyed more servants than many realize.
The Bible tells a story that should make every Christian stop and examine their heart.
Not because it condemns us.
Because it exposes us.
In Luke 10, Jesus enters a home where two sisters respond very differently to His presence.
Martha becomes consumed with serving.
Mary sits at His feet.
The text says:
“But Martha was distracted with much serving.”
The Greek word translated “distracted” is περισπάω (perispaō).
It carries the idea of being pulled apart, dragged in different directions, overoccupied, and inwardly fragmented.
Martha was not distracted by sin.
She was distracted by service.
She was not pursuing evil.
She was pursuing ministry.
And that is precisely what makes this story so uncomfortable.
Jesus did not rebuke her for serving.
He rebuked her because serving had become more important than being with Him.
“Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary.”
One thing.
Not ten things.
Not a hundred things.
One thing.
The Lord of Heaven was sitting in her living room, and she was too busy preparing for Him to enjoy Him.
How many believers are doing the same thing today?
Preparing sermons while neglecting prayer.
Building ministries while neglecting worship.
Helping others heal while carrying unhealed wounds.
Teaching Scripture while starving spiritually.
Working for Jesus while forgetting to walk with Jesus.
The Bible contains an even more sobering warning.
In Matthew 7:22-23, Jesus describes people standing before Him on the Day of Judgment.
Their ministry résumé is astonishing.
“Did we not prophesy in Your name?”
“Cast out demons in Your name?”
“Do many mighty works in Your name?”
Notice what they point to.
Not relationship.
Results.
Not intimacy.
Achievements.
Not communion.
Performance.
Yet Jesus responds with one of the most terrifying statements in Scripture:
“I never knew you.”
The Greek phrase is:

οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς
(oudepote egnōn hymas)
“I never knew you.”
The word ἔγνων (egnōn) comes from γινώσκω (ginōskō), which often describes relational, experiential knowledge.
Not mere information.
Not acquaintance.
Relationship.
Jesus was not saying He lacked awareness of their existence.
He was exposing the absence of intimacy.
They had ministry.
But they did not have Him.
That distinction should shake every believer.
Because ministry can sometimes become a hiding place.
A person can stay so busy serving others that they never allow God to deal with themselves.
Activity becomes anesthesia.
Productivity becomes avoidance.
Religious success becomes camouflage.
We become experts at helping everyone else while quietly ignoring what God wants to heal within us.
King Saul offers another heartbreaking example.
At first, Saul appeared devoted to God's mission.
Yet over time, he became more concerned with preserving his position than preserving his relationship with God.
When confronted by the prophet Samuel, Saul's greatest concern was often how he appeared before people.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly reveal a painful truth.
Outward obedience without inward surrender eventually collapses.
God told Samuel:
“Man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.”
The Hebrew word for heart is לֵב (lev).
In biblical thought, the lev is not merely emotion.
It is the center of desire, devotion, will, thought, and affection.
God was not primarily examining Saul's ministry.
He was examining Saul's heart.
And God still does the same today.
One of the greatest dangers in Christian leadership is confusing spiritual output with spiritual health.
They are not the same thing.
A pastor may preach powerful sermons while battling private emptiness.
A worship leader may lead thousands into God's presence while personally feeling distant.
A ministry volunteer may serve every week while neglecting personal prayer.
A Christian content creator may post daily encouragement while secretly feeling disconnected from Christ.
The fruit people see is not always proof of the roots beneath.
Jesus understood this danger.
That is why He frequently withdrew.
Again and again, Scripture records Him leaving crowds behind.
Leaving opportunities behind.
Leaving demands behind.
Leaving ministry behind.
To pray.
To be alone with the Father.
If anyone had a legitimate reason to stay busy, it was Jesus.
Yet He repeatedly prioritized communion over activity.
The Son of God refused to allow ministry to replace intimacy.
Why do we think we can survive doing what even Jesus refused to do?
The irony is painful.
Many Christians dream of hearing:
“Well done, good and faithful servant.”
Yet we often spend so much time being servants that we forget how to be sons and daughters.
God never intended relationship to become a casualty of service.
The first commandment was never ministry.
The first commandment was love.
When Jesus summarized the Law, He began with this:
“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart.”
The Hebrew word behind this concept of love throughout the Old Testament is often אָהַב (ahav).
Not cold duty.
Not religious obligation.
Love.
Affection.
Devotion.
Relationship.
God has always desired more than our labor.
He desires us.
This truth becomes even clearer in the final book of Scripture.
Jesus addresses the church in Ephesus.
Their theology was strong.
Their discernment was strong.
Their perseverance was strong.
Their ministry was active.
Everything looked impressive.
Yet Jesus says:
“I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first.”
Imagine hearing those words.
Not from critics.
Not from enemies.
From Jesus Himself.
The tragedy was not doctrinal failure.
The tragedy was relational drift.
They had preserved truth while losing tenderness.
They had maintained ministry while losing intimacy.
They had remembered their mission while forgetting their first love.
Perhaps that is where some readers find themselves today.
Not in open rebellion.
Not trapped in scandal.
Not abandoning the faith.
Just tired.
Dry.
Busy.
Spiritually exhausted.
Still serving.
Still showing up.
Still carrying responsibilities.
Yet secretly wondering where the closeness went.
If that is you, hear this clearly.
God is not asking you to abandon ministry.
He is inviting you back to Himself.
Before He wants your platform, He wants your heart.
Before He wants your gifts, He wants your presence.
Before He wants your service, He wants your surrender.
The Gospel itself reminds us of this.
Jesus did not die merely to recruit workers.
He died to reconcile people to God.
The cross was not about creating employees.
It was about restoring relationship.
The goal of Christianity has never been ministry success.
The goal has always been union with Christ.
The invitation remains exactly what it has always been:
“Follow Me.”
Not merely work for Me.
Not merely speak about Me.
Not merely build for Me.
Follow Me.
Perhaps today is the day to close the laptop for a moment.
Put down the ministry plans.
Turn off the notifications.
Open the Scriptures.
Bow your head.
And simply sit at His feet again.
Not because you need another sermon.
Not because you need another strategy.
Not because you need another accomplishment.
Because you need Him.
And maybe that is what your soul has been missing all along.
Be honest. This hit harder than many expected.
One day, the greatest regret will not be that we did too little for God—but that we spent so much time doing things for Him that we forgot to spend time with Him.
